Kaneki product layer: idea to MVP

Proposal · kaneki harness

Kaneki product layer: idea to MVP

A gated layer that sits above /kaneki-flow. It takes a raw idea to an MVP through one six-stage spine, either spec-first (decide, then build) or prototype-first (build to learn, then promote), and ends with ticket files kaneki already knows how to build. It reuses Matt Pocock's MIT-licensed planning skills where they fit.

  • Updated2026-11-23
  • Scopeagentic-workflows @ main ff10094
  • StatusDraft for your decision

Recommendation

In short

Add a product layer to kaneki. It runs once per product, not once per ticket, and ends by writing tickets/<id>.md files that /kaneki-flow already builds. It is one six-stage spine (Frame → Discover → MVP cut → Spec → Slice → Build) with two main ways through stage 2:

  • spec-first: decide, then build, using Pocock's wayfinder map;
  • prototype-first: build to learn, then decide at a promote gate.

A lite lane skips discovery for small ideas.

  1. Kaneki starts at a ticket that already exists. Its first node, prepare, copies a ticket file that a user wrote. Nothing in the harness produces that file. S2S3 VERIFIED
  2. Pocock's skills cover the engineering half of "idea → tickets". Grilling, wayfinder, spec, tracer-bullet tickets and throwaway prototypes. S6 VERIFIED
  3. They do not cover the product half. None of the 16 skills I read mentions an MVP, SaaS, pricing, billing, a target user or a success metric. VERIFIED for those 16 of the 26 skills.
  4. The two flows differ only in how they remove uncertainty. Spec-first decides each open question on a map. Prototype-first builds until you would use the thing. From the MVP cut onwards they share the same gates, the same spec and slice steps, and the same output, so a product can switch lanes without losing work (see How the two flows relate).
  5. Product type is a set of dimensions, not one label. Who uses it, who pays, single or multi-tenant, deployment and money are picked separately. That lets "internal software sold as SaaS to local businesses" be described exactly, instead of forced into either "internal tool" or "SaaS".
  6. The prototype lane goes beyond Pocock on purpose. His prototype is "throwaway code that answers a question". S16 The prototype lane can also evolve the prototype into the product, so it is guarded by a promote gate that you approve.
  7. Build it in three steps: skills and files only, then the driver and its gates, then the board. Each step is usable on its own.

Where kaneki starts today, and what is missing upstream

The kaneki graph is built for one change at a time. Its trace begins at prepare and moves through analysis, plan, code, review, evidence and delivery. S2 With the local-file tracker, the ticket is "a markdown file the user writes". S3

The tickets in this workspace show where that file comes from today. P1-T01 cites a build plan, its part plans and a decision list, all written outside the harness. S4 So the hardest thinking happens with no gates, no decision log and no receipts: what the product is for, who it serves, what counts as done, and how it splits into tickets.

The gap in one sentenceKaneki makes sure each ticket is built right, but nothing makes sure the tickets add up to the right product.

What Matt Pocock's skills give us

The repo mattpocock/skills holds 26 small skills under the MIT license, so we can adapt them as long as we keep the copyright notice. S10 His router skill sets the main flow as interview, then spec, then tickets, then build. For "a huge, foggy effort: a greenfield project", it sends you to /wayfinder first. S6

Wayfinder: decisions before deliverables

Wayfinder plans work that is too big for one session as a map of decision tickets. Each ticket is a question, and closing it records a decision. It does not deliver code. S5

  • The map is one index with five parts: Destination, Notes, Decisions so far, Not yet specified (the "fog") and Out of scope.
  • Ticket types:
    • Research: the agent works alone.
    • Prototype and Grilling: the human is in the loop.
    • Task: manual work, such as provisioning access, that has to happen before a decision can be made.
  • Fog vs ticket: an unknown becomes a ticket once you "can state the question precisely now", even if you cannot answer it yet. S5
  • One ticket per session, except research tickets. This keeps each decision inside a fresh context.

The rest of the chain

Pocock skills relevant to idea → tickets, and what to do with each

SkillWhat it doesVerdict for kaneki
grillingInterviews you in rounds over a "design tree". Each question carries a recommended answer. Facts are the agent's job; decisions are yours. S7✓ port as the interview engine for every HITL step
domain-modelingKeeps GLOSSARY.md and ADRs up to date.✓ port; the glossary feeds kaneki's requirement-analysis
wayfinderThe decision map described above. S5✓ port, with the map stored in local files instead of GitHub issues

to-questionnaireTurns a decision you can't answer alone into a questionnaire for someone else. S15✓ port as the customer-evidence ticket
to-specTurns the conversation into a spec with "no interview, just synthesis". Picks the highest test seam: "the ideal number is one". S8✓ port, plus MVP and product-type sections

Design notePocock keeps the source of truth on the issue tracker and, by name, criticises frameworks that "try to help by owning the process". S11 Kaneki is a process-owning framework on purpose: gates, receipts, a decision log. The port therefore keeps his techniques (grilling, fog, tracer bullets) and puts them under kaneki's gates.

Product type is a set of dimensions

A personal script, a team tool and a paid SaaS need very different MVPs. Today that difference lives only in your head. The proposal writes it down as dimensions, each chosen on its own in the brief:

  • each choice adds questions to ask, defaults to propose and launch checks for the final gate;
  • common combinations are saved as presets.

This follows the existing rule "the graph is generic; the project is data". S1 Dimensions add questions and checks, never graph nodes.

Dimensions and what each choice adds

Who uses ityou · known staff · the public · developersRoles, devices (shared tablet, phone), skill level, language
Who paysnobody · your employer · a client (contract) · each customer (subscription)Pricing, billing, trial and contract questions. If the payer is not the user, a separate buyer goal.
Customers of the customernone · yes (bookings, orders)A third group with its own goal and privacy needs
Tenancysingle · one copy per client · multi-tenantData isolation, sign-up, migrating data in and out
Deploymentyour machine · one server · cloud · app stores · registryOps, backups, monitoring and release launch checks
Where it is soldcountry / regionResearch tickets for local payment methods, invoices, tax and personal-data law

When you are not the source of truth

If the users or the payer are other people, many answers must come from them, not from you. Wayfinder already insists that "the agent never stands in for the human's side" of a ticket. S5 The proposal adds a fifth decision-ticket type, customer evidence:

  • the agent writes an interview script with Pocock's to-questionnaire, which targets "the gap between what the recipient knows and what the user needs" S15;
  • you run the interview;
  • the ticket records what was said, in product/evidence/.

The MVP gate then requires every must item to cite either evidence or your brief.

The presets themselves are untested proposals. INFERRED: whether one schema can hold them all cleanly needs a prototype.

Two flows on one spine

Every product goes through the same six stages and ends in the same place: approved tickets that /kaneki-flow builds. What differs is stage 2, Discover, where the uncertainty gets removed:

  • full: decide first, on a map (spec-first);
  • prototype: build first and learn from using it (prototype-first);
  • lite: skip discovery, because nothing is uncertain.
Hover or tap a stage: 1 Frame2 Discover3 MVP cut4 Spec5 Slice6 Build

Which lane to start in

Your situationLaneWhy
Small and clear: you could write the tickets todayliteNothing to discover. One gate, then build.
Unclear, but "I'll know it when I see it", and you are the main user or judgeprototypeBuilding is the fastest way to find out. Your reaction is the evidence.
Big or foggy, or the answers belong to other people (customers, law, partners, a client)fullA prototype cannot answer "will shops pay?" or "is this legal?". Decision tickets with evidence can.

Spec-first flow: decide, then build

This is the full lane. It is built for efforts too big or too dependent on other people to hold in one session. Every stage ends at a gate you approve, and each gate's artifact cites the ones before it.

  1. Frame: what and why/kaneki-idea

    Grill the raw idea using Pocock's grilling rounds, which put a recommended answer on every question. S7 The output is brief.md:

    • problem and purpose;
    • buyer, users and customers-of-the-customer;
    • the dimensions;
    • one goal per group;
    • constraints and non-goals.

    The dimensions add their questions here. A paid product cannot pass the gate until pricing intent and data handling have an answer, even if that answer is "decide later".

    Gate G-briefYou approve the brief.
  2. Discover by map: clear the fog/kaneki-map

    Wayfinder, ported to local files. product/map/MAP.md holds:

    • Destination, taken from the brief;
    • Decisions so far;
    • Not yet specified;
    • Out of scope.

    Each precisely stated unknown becomes D-NNN-*.md, with one of five types: research, prototype, grilling, task or customer evidence. Tickets carry blocking edges. You resolve one ticket per session, except research tickets, which run in parallel. S5

    ExampleD-004 evidence: do salon owners take bookings by phone or Zalo? · D-007 prototype: is the booking grid usable on a phone?
  3. MVP cut: the smallest thing that proves the goalnew, not in Pocock

    The agent lists every capability that came up and proposes three groups:

    • must: each item cites a goal in the brief, or evidence;
    • later: each item names its milestone;
    • never.

    mvp.md also names the riskiest assumption (built first), the walking skeleton and the launch checks that come from the dimensions.

    Gate G-mvpItems in later or never cannot become tickets without reopening this gate.
  4. Spec: a buildable plan and a repo/kaneki-spec

    to-spec, ported: synthesis, with no new interview. S8 spec.md covers:

    • numbered user stories;
    • implementation decisions;
    • as few test seams as possible;
    • out of scope.

    Stack choices are recorded as ADRs. For a new product this stage also bootstraps the repo: scaffold, CI, the my-git branch model and one passing test. It then runs /kaneki-onboarding, which needs a repository to scan.

    Gate G-specYou approve the spec and the stack ADRs.
  5. Slice: milestones and tickets/kaneki-slice

    to-tickets, ported: tracer-bullet slices, each "a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer". S9 The default milestones are:

    • M0: the walking skeleton;
    • M1: the MVP must list;
    • M2: the launch checks.

    Paid products add M3 (scale). You review the list before any file is written.

    Gate G-ticketsYou approve the roadmap and the ticket set.
  6. Build & launch/kaneki-flow · /kaneki-ship

    Each ticket runs through the unchanged ticket graph. The product layer adds a next-ticket view (open tickets whose blockers are done) and the launch gate: every M1 ticket is deliverable-ready, and every launch check has evidence. A retro then turns usage and surprises into new decision tickets.

    Gate G-launchYou approve the launch and record the first value of the goal metric.

Prototype-first flow: build to learn, then decide

This is the prototype lane, for an idea you can't specify yet but will recognise when you use it. The gates are moved to after discovery: nothing slows the prototype down, and nothing from it reaches a real ticket until you have decided what it becomes.

  1. Spark: half a page, about 10 minutes, no gate/kaneki-idea --prototype

    A short grilling session produces a half-page brief.md:

    • who it is for;
    • the one job it does;
    • what "it works" means, as something you can check;
    • the dimensions, as a first guess.
    Example"I can log an expense from my phone in 5 seconds and see the month's total."
  2. Discover by prototype loop: build, use, write down what you learned/kaneki-proto
    • The agent builds fast on a prototype/<name> branch or in a throwaway repo. It uses real-ish data, and adds tests and auth only if the idea depends on them.
    • After each round you use it. The agent adds a few lines to product/learnings.md: what worked, what felt wrong, what to change next, and which screens or flows you actually used.
    • It reuses Pocock's prototype techniques, such as several UI variants switchable on one route, or a clickable state machine. S16

    You stop when you would really use it, or when the idea is not worth it. Killing an idea here is a success, and it gets one line in decisions.jsonl.

  3. Promote gate, then MVP cutthe one decision that matters

    You choose what the prototype becomes: rebuild, evolve or kill. The agent recommends one using the checklist below. Then the normal MVP cut runs. In this lane it is usually "the prototype, minus what you never used", and learnings.md is its evidence.

    Gate G-promote + G-mvpBoth are recorded with your approval, the same way a ticket gate is.
  4. Spec: written from the prototype
    • Rebuild: the agent reverse-engineers spec.md from the flows you actually used plus learnings.md. Screenshots become the acceptance criteria. Then it bootstraps a clean repo, as in spec-first.
    • Evolve: the spec describes the prototype as it is, plus the gaps. /kaneki-onboarding runs on the prototype repo, and the prototype branch is merged into develop/base through a normal PR.
  5. Slice: hardening first when evolving
    • For evolve, M0 is a hardening milestone: tests at the main seams, error handling, and whatever auth, data safety and backups the dimensions require. Feature tickets come after it.
    • For rebuild, slicing is the same as in spec-first, with the prototype as the reference.
  6. Build & launch: identical to spec-first

Checklist the agent uses to recommend rebuild or evolve

Question about the prototypePoints to evolvePoints to rebuild
Is it on the stack you would ship?yesno, or a demo-only tool
Does the data model fit the dimensions (e.g. multi-tenant)?yessingle-user model for a multi-tenant product
Can the main flows be tested without rewriting them?clear seamslogic tangled into the UI
How many times did direction change during the loop?0–1several, with leftovers in the code
Who will rely on it?youpaying customers, their data
Main riskA prototype that quietly becomes production without anyone deciding it should. To block that, /kaneki-flow refuses a ticket whose repository is a prototype/* branch with no recorded promote decision.

How the two flows relate

They are two lanes of one graph, not two products. The same driver, the same files and the same gates apply from the MVP cut onwards. They differ in one stage and in what counts as evidence.

Spec-first vs prototype-first, stage by stage

StageSpec-first (full)Prototype-first (prototype)Shared?
1 Framefull brief, gatedhalf-page spark, no gatesame brief.md format
2 Discoverdecision tickets on a mapbuild, use, learn loopdifferent
Evidence for must itemsresolved tickets, customer evidencelearnings.md, flows you usedsame rule: every item cites something
3 MVP cutgatepromote gate, then the same gate✓
4 Specwritten forward from decisionswritten backward from the prototype✓ same spec.md template
5 SliceM0 = walking skeletonM0 = skeleton (rebuild) or hardening (evolve)✓ same ticket format
6 Buildunchanged /kaneki-flow and /kaneki-ship✓
Time to first working thingslow (after G-spec)fast (day one)
Can answer questions owned by others?yes, via evidence ticketsonly what you can judge yourself

They nest inside each other

A prototype inside the map

A map ticket of type prototype is a small prototype loop scoped to one question, and always thrown away (Pocock's original meaning). Example: D-007, "is the booking grid usable on a phone?"

A map inside a prototype

When the loop hits a question you can't judge yourself ("will owners pay 200k/month?"), the agent writes it as a decision ticket. A small map then grows next to the prototype instead of guessing.

Switching lanes

Switching lanes is recorded like the ticket graph's sdlc lane --set … --reason, and nothing done so far is lost. S1

From → toWhenWhat carries over
lite → prototype / fullThe "clear" idea turns out unclear, or bigger than about 5 ticketsBrief; the MVP/spec page becomes a draft
prototype → fullKey answers belong to other people, or several foggy unknowns appearBrief (now gated), learnings.md as map notes, the prototype as an asset on map tickets
full → prototypeThe map keeps stalling on "how should it feel" questionsResolved decisions become constraints for the loop
After launchEach new milestone re-enters stage 2Everything. Pick the lane per milestone, e.g. a full product can explore one new feature with prototype.

Worked example: internal software sold as SaaS to local businesses

A booking and staff-schedule app for small salons, sold as a monthly subscription. This is the case that breaks a one-label product type, so it shows how the pieces combine.

  1. Frame

    Preset local-business SaaS: staff use it, the owner pays, customers book, multi-tenant, cloud, sold in one country. The brief sets three goals:

    • owner: renews after the pilot;
    • staff: use it every shift;
    • customers: book without calling.
  2. Discover: full lane with prototype tickets inside

    The answers belong to shop owners, so this is spec-first. The map has three kinds of ticket:

    • Customer evidence: interview 5 owners about how they book today and what they would pay.
    • Prototype: a clickable booking grid shown to those owners.
    • Research: local payment methods, e-invoice and tax rules, personal-data law, and multi-tenant from day one vs one copy per shop.

    OPEN I have not checked any legal rule. Each one is a research ticket.

  3. MVP cut
    • Must: bookings, the staff schedule, importing the existing client list from Excel or paper, owner/staff roles, and daily backups. Each item cites an interview.
    • Later: online payment, SMS reminders.
    • Never (for now): inventory.
  4. Milestones
    • M0: skeleton. Login, one shop, one booking end to end.
    • M1: pilot MVP with 1–3 partner shops.
    • M2: sellable. Self sign-up, billing, data export.
    • M3: support and monitoring.
  5. Launch gate

    The gate is the pilot, not a public launch: the pilot shops used it for N weeks, and the owners' renewal decision is recorded.

If you instead mean custom software for a single business, hosted for them, use the custom client app preset. That means single tenant, a contract instead of billing, and that one client as the only source of evidence. The same flow applies, with fewer launch checks.

What ends up on disk

Everything is plain markdown in the workspace, next to sdlc.profile.json, and none of it depends on a GitHub tracker. That suits this workspace, where the agent does not run gh.

<workspace>/
├─ product/
│  ├─ brief.md               purpose · buyer/users/customers · dimensions · goals   (G-brief)
│  ├─ GLOSSARY.md  adr/      domain words and decisions (domain-modeling)
│  ├─ map/MAP.md             full lane: destination · decisions · fog · out of scope
│  ├─ map/D-001-*.md …       decision tickets: type, question, blocked-by, resolution
│  ├─ evidence/              customer-evidence scripts and answers
│  ├─ learnings.md           prototype lane: one entry per round
│  ├─ mvp.md                 must / later / never · riskiest bet · launch checks   (G-mvp)
│  ├─ spec.md                user stories · decisions · test seams                 (G-spec)
│  ├─ roadmap.md             milestones with ticket ids                             (G-tickets)
│  └─ state.json  decisions.jsonl   lane, gates, promote decision (driver format)
├─ tickets/M1-T03.md …       handed to /kaneki-flow unchanged
└─ sdlc.profile.json         written by /kaneki-onboarding after bootstrap

The handoff contract: a ticket kaneki can build

Tickets use the sections the workspace already uses: Kind · Part · Size · Depends on, then Problem, Expected, Done when, Out of scope. S4 They add back-references, so requirement-analysis can treat the spec as a primary source:

# M1-T03: Owner imports the client list from Excel

Kind: feature · Part: M1 pilot MVP · Size: M · Depends on: M0-T01 · Lane: full
Source: product/spec.md US-4 · product/mvp.md must-3 · evidence/E-002 · ADR-0002

How to build it

  1. Step 1: skills, presets and files, no driver change~1 worktree
    • skills/kaneki-product/ with entry points idea, proto, map, spec and slice. They port grilling, domain-modeling, prototype, to-questionnaire, wayfinder, to-spec and to-tickets, with the MIT notice and a NOTICE listing each source and the upstream version.
    • presets/*.json plus a dimensions schema in contracts/.
    • Templates for the brief, learnings, map, MVP and roadmap.
    • Build the prototype and lite lanes first: they are the cheapest and the most likely to be used on a new idea.

    Done when: one real idea goes through the prototype lane to tickets/*.md, and /kaneki-flow runs the first ticket unedited.

  2. Step 2: the product graph in the driver
    • graph/product.json with the three lanes.
    • sdlc product init|status|gate|lane.
    • The gates (including promote), and the kaneki-flow refusal for unpromoted prototype branches.
    • Then the full lane's map and customer-evidence tickets.

    Done when: the gates refuse to close without your approval, the same way gate does for tickets. S1

  3. Step 3: board and loop
    • sdlc web product view: lane, map frontier or prototype rounds, milestone progress, the next unblocked ticket.
    • Launch-check evidence.
    • The retro writes the next milestone's stage-2 work.
Risks
  • Ceremony. Too many gates for small ideas. The lite and prototype lanes exist for that.
  • Prototype debt. Evolve can carry shortcuts into production. The hardening milestone and the checklist are the guard.
  • Context. Pocock wants grilling, spec and tickets in "one unbroken context window". S6 Kaneki's stages hand off through files, so every stage must work from the brief, map, learnings and ADRs alone.
  • Upstream drift. Pocock renames skills often. Port the techniques, record the upstream version, and don't vendor the files.

Decisions I need from you

  1. Placement. Should this live inside the kaneki harness, or in a sibling harness/product-kit that only writes kaneki tickets? I recommend inside kaneki. OPEN
  2. Lane order. Should step 1 build prototype + lite first, as proposed, or full first? OPEN
  3. Evolve allowed for paid products? One option is to require rebuild whenever someone other than you pays. I recommend allowing evolve, but only with the hardening milestone. OPEN
  4. Presets for v1. Are the six above the right set? OPEN
  5. First trial idea. Which real idea do we run through the prototype lane first? OPEN
